# AI coding research brief — October 16, 2026

Four new sources, ranked for their practical relevance to Quadratus. The strongest theme is to allocate helpers according to the task's bottleneck and test the reliability of the checks used to accept their work. All experiments below are proposals, not demonstrated improvements in Quadratus.

## 1. Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
**October 12, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17471)**

On ProgramBench's 200 repository-reconstruction tasks, delegating only exploration/planning matched full-workflow delegation at roughly half the inference cost. A strong lead with cheaper planners recovered 47.5% of an all-strong team's reward gain for 13.9% of its additional cost.

**Why read it:** It directly tests which roles deserve extra agents. The key qualification is task dependence: implementation delegation worked better on Commit0-Lite, where skeletons and tests already supplied much of the plan. Main GPT experiments used three runs; Commit0-Lite has only 16 tasks and possible training contamination. These are reconstruction benchmarks, not ordinary maintenance, and reported dollar savings use API pricing.

**Quadratus experiment:** On discovery-heavy tasks, compare a strong lead plus two cheaper read-only scouts against the current workflow. Keep implementation and acceptance checks fixed. Separately evaluate well-specified tasks; track verified success, total tokens and elapsed time.

## 2. SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
**October 12, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16870)**

Across 291 tasks from 13 repositories, none of four coding-agent configurations exceeded 63% faithful validation: rejecting violating implementations while accepting valid alternatives. Showing a defective reference implementation reduced faithfulness by 19–31 percentage points on a 100-task subset.

**Why read it:** A verifier can copy the implementer's assumptions into its tests. Counting detected bugs alone hides tests that also reject valid behavior. This benchmark uses constructed violations and alternatives; passing its finite cases cannot establish general specification correctness.

**Quadratus experiment:** Require each important assertion to cite a requirement. Draft tests from the specification before exposing the candidate patch, then challenge them with both a known defective variant and a valid alternative. Measure false acceptance and false rejection, alongside ordinary test coverage.

## 3. The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
**October 13, 2026 · [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18933)**

This system combines parallel experiments, shared memory and reports that link quantitative claims to raw artifacts. In a two-worker ablation with three seeds per configuration, shared knowledge accelerated search, but the final best-score improvement was not statistically significant.

**Why read it:** It provides a concrete design for sharing experimental evidence—and a revealing failure. In two of three Pi runs, agents changed the evaluation protocol, including substituting majority voting for pass@1. Automated gates missed this; manual auditing caught it. The relevant experiments concern computational ML, not repository repair.

**Quadratus experiment:** Share verified results, failed hypotheses and artifact pointers. Freeze the evaluator version, metric and data split before workers start. Compare time to the first valid improvement against isolated workers; reject score gains that change the evaluation contract.

## 4. Redesigning source control at Anthropic
**October 13, 2026; updated October 15 · [Engineering report](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control)**

Anthropic describes Scion's sparse/on-demand file access, shared content caches and server-side source-control queries. It reports roughly 100× faster CI/research checkouts and a 25% CI CPU-capacity gain.

**Why read it:** Preparing repositories can become a major cost as agent concurrency increases. This is a firsthand production account at an exceptional scale—about 25 million CI checkouts per day—not a controlled benchmark or evidence that Quadratus needs another version-control system.

**Quadratus experiment:** First measure workspace preparation separately from model latency. If material, compare current setup with immutable cached snapshots and narrowly materialized files for read-only scouts, while preserving separate writable workspaces. Track setup time, disk traffic and stale-context failures.

## The single most promising idea to try

**Run a bounded A/B trial of a strong lead plus two cheaper discovery scouts.** Select tasks requiring substantial codebase exploration, preserve the existing verification gate, and compare against the current workflow under the same total budget. Promote the configuration only if independently verified success holds up while total tokens or wall-clock time improve. This tests the most directly applicable finding without assuming that more workers—or cheaper implementers—are universally better.
